newsitem.title: USA: Oakland, Calif. taxable bonds single-A - Fitch.
newsitem.headline: Oakland, Calif. taxable bonds single-A - Fitch.

text.p: Oakland, CA.'s $436,623,154 taxable pension obligation bonds, series 1997 are rated 'A' by Fitch Investors Service.

The bonds are scheduled to be sold on a negotiated basis through a syndicate led by PaineWebber Inc. on or about Feb. 11. The bonds are dated Feb. 1, 1997. The sub-series A bonds mature as follows: the $395,455,000 current interest bonds mature serially from Dec. 15, 1998 through 2009; $25,913,154 capital appreciation bonds (CABs) mature Dec. 15, 2010. The $15,255,000 current interest sub-series B bonds mature serially from Dec. 15, 1998 through 2000. The current interest bonds are dated Feb. 1, 1997; the CABs are dated on the delivery date.

The bonds are not subject to redemption prior to maturity. Bond proceeds will be used to refund a city debenture issued by the city to the City of Oakland Police and Fire Retirement System (PFRS), evidencing a portion of the city's unfunded liability to this pension fund. The bonds are secured by payments from any city revenue, although the sub- series A bonds will be paid, to the extent available, from tax override levy monies.

The city's obligation to make annual pension fund payments, including amounts to amortize the unfunded accrued liability, and its obligation to pay debt service on these bonds, is imposed by law and enforceable against the city. The 'A' rating is based on the city's high general fund balances, growing property tax base, moderate but growing debt burden and the legal strength of the pension obligation. Budget balancing remains tight. The tax and employment base have diversified, although labor force and employment growth has been sluggish. Future budget gaps are forecast. However, the city has shown flexibility in closing prior gaps. Oakland is California's eighth largest city and is a transportation hub, with nine major U.S. and California highways converging there and high-speed light rail transit provided by the Bay Area Rapid Transit.

The city is home to one of three major commercial airports serving the Oakland- San Francisco Bay area and one of the primary sea terminals for cargo moving between the U.S. and the Pacific Rim, Latin America and Europe. The tax and employment base is diverse and able to support the county's operating and capital needs. The tax base has shown healthy growth of 26% over the past five years. While the unemployment rate has historically been higher than those of Alameda County, the state and the nation, it has fallen every year since 1992. The closure of virtually all the naval facilities in Alameda County and of the Oakland Army Base could result in the loss of 24,600 military and civilian jobs. Efforts are under way to mitigate the impact of the closures. Oakland's debt levels have been moderate, but will increase with the issuance of these bonds.

Direct debt per capita, including these bonds, is $2,047, and overall debt is above average at 7.0% of assessed value or $2,813 per capita. Without these pension obligation bonds, debt is more moderate, at $918 per capita on a direct basis and $1,684 per capita or 4.2% of assessed value overall. The city is a participant with Alameda County in the Oakland-Alameda County Coliseum Authority, which has issued bonds for the remodeling of the Oakland Coliseum and construction of a new Oakland Arena. Financial operations remain sound despite continued expenditure pressure on city revenues. Although the city has recorded general fund deficits in four of last five fiscal years, fund balances have been strong. In fiscal 1996, the city recorded a $9.7 million deficit, which reduced the ending fund balance to $28.5 million from $38.1 million in fiscal 1995. The $28.5 million fund balance was still a high 10% of general fund expenditures and transfers out.
